title: Counter with CBC-MAC (CCM)
summary: Defines Counter with CBC-MAC (CCM), a way of using a block cipher to both encrypt data and authenticate it in one scheme. It is specified for ciphers with 128-bit blocks, such as AES. Combining secrecy and tamper detection in a single mode makes it convenient for protocols to use.

plainLanguage.summary: Think of sealing a letter in an envelope that is both scrambled so nobody can read it and stamped so you can tell if anyone opened it. This recipe does both jobs together using one secret key.

questions: what happens if you reuse a nonce in ccm
subtitle: A block cipher mode that encrypts a message and authenticates it, plus extra header data, with one key.

tldr.problem: Protocols need to keep data secret and also detect tampering, and doing the two jobs with separate schemes is clumsy.
tldr.mechanism: CCM computes a CBC-MAC over the message and optional additional data, then encrypts the message and the MAC with counter (CTR) mode, all with the same key and a unique nonce per message.
tldr.outcome: Each message grows only by the authentication field of 4 to 16 octets. Reusing a nonce under one key destroys the security of the mode.

today: RFC 3610 is an Informational RFC and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the RFC definition of CCM as published in September 2003.

sections.title: What CCM Is
sections.content:
Counter with CBC-MAC (CCM) is a generic authenticated encryption block cipher mode. It is defined only for 128-bit block ciphers such as AES. The RFC says the design principles could be applied to other block sizes, but those would need their own specifications.

CCM combines two older building blocks: CBC-MAC to compute an authentication value, and CTR mode to encrypt. Both use the same block cipher key.
sections.plainLanguage: CCM is a recipe that uses a lock-and-stamp machine with 16-letter blocks. It mixes two simple tricks so one secret key does both scrambling and checking.

sections.title: Parameters and Inputs
sections.content:
Two parameters shape each use of CCM. M is the size of the authentication field, and valid values are 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16 octets. It trades message expansion against the chance that an attacker can modify a message undetected; the RFC recommends choosing M of at least 8. L is the size of the length field, from 2 to 8 octets (L=1 is reserved), and it trades maximum message size against nonce size.

To protect a message you supply four inputs: a key K; a nonce N of 15-L octets that MUST be unique within the scope of that key; the message m of fewer than 2^(8L) octets; and additional authenticated data a of fewer than 2^64 octets. The additional data is authenticated but not encrypted and is not included in the output. It suits plaintext packet headers, and may be empty.

Using the same nonce for two different messages under the same key destroys the security properties of the mode.
sections.plainLanguage: You choose how long the stamp is and how big a message can be. You also give each message its own one-time number, and you must never repeat it.

sections.title: Authenticating and Encrypting
sections.content:
First CCM builds a sequence of blocks B_0, B_1, ... B_n and runs CBC-MAC over them. B_0 holds a flags octet, the nonce and the message length. If there is additional data, its encoded length and its bytes follow in 16-octet blocks, zero-padded; then the message blocks follow, also zero-padded. The tag T is the first M bytes of the final cipher output.

Encryption uses CTR mode. Counter blocks A_i hold a flags octet (equal to L'), the nonce and a counter i, and the key stream is S_i = E(K, A_i). The message is XORed with S_1, S_2 and so on; S_0 is not used for the message. Instead the authentication value is U = T XOR the first M bytes of S_0. The output is the encrypted message followed by U.

The flags octet in B_0 is 64*Adata + 8*M' + L', where M' is (M-2)/2 and L' is L-1. The A blocks carry zero in the bits where B_0 has the non-zero M' encoding, so every A block differs from B_0.
sections.plainLanguage: Step one makes a short fingerprint of the whole message. Step two scrambles the message using a never-ending stream of secret-looking numbers, and scrambles the fingerprint too.

sections.title: Decryption and Limits
sections.content:
To decrypt, the receiver needs the key, the nonce, the additional data and the encrypted message. It recomputes the key stream to recover the message and T, then recomputes the CBC-MAC and checks T. If T is wrong, the receiver MUST NOT reveal anything except the fact that it is incorrect, not even the decrypted message or the value T. The recipient MUST verify the CBC-MAC before releasing any information such as the plaintext.

A single key has a usage limit: the total number of block cipher encryption operations in the CBC-MAC and encryption together cannot exceed 2^61. The RFC says this still allows nearly 2^64 octets to be protected. Senders MUST stay within it.
sections.plainLanguage: When a letter arrives, you first check the stamp. If the stamp is wrong, you throw the letter away and tell nobody what was inside.

sections.title: Security, Nonces and Rationale
sections.content:
The RFC cites a security proof by Jakob Jonsson, presented at SAC 2002, which shows CCM gives confidentiality and authenticity in line with other proposed authenticated encryption modes such as OCB. Encrypting T avoids CBC-MAC collision attacks. The same key can safely serve both functions because all A blocks differ from each other and from B_0.

For nonces, the main requirement is uniqueness within a key. A common technique is to number messages sequentially, as is already done for replay detection in protocols such as IPsec ESP. The RFC also warns of precomputation attacks, which are collision attacks on the cipher key: with a 128-bit key and one nonce used under many keys, the attacker's work drops to about 2^64 steps. A 256-bit key forces at least 2^128 precomputations. Adding random bytes or a sender's Ethernet address to the nonce can help, but the RFC says such measures need careful analysis and almost never entirely prevent these attacks, and recommends a larger key where possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The main safety rule is never reuse the one-time number. A bigger secret key also makes cheating much harder.

sections.title: Performance and Properties
sections.content:
Speed depends on the block cipher. In hardware, for large packets, CCM is roughly as fast as CBC encryption mode. Protecting an empty message with no additional data takes two block cipher encryption operations; each message block takes two more, and each block of additional data takes one more. CCM uses only the block cipher's encrypt direction, which can save code or hardware size, and adds only the authentication bits to the message.

The RFC also lists limits: encryption can be parallelized but authentication cannot, and the message length must be known at the start. The document ends with 24 packet test vectors using AES; some use an eight octet authentication value and others a ten octet one.
sections.plainLanguage: CCM is quick because it only needs the scrambling half of the cipher, and the stamp adds just a few extra bytes.

viz.caption: FLAGS OCTET IN THE FIRST AUTHENTICATION BLOCK B_0

items.label: Adata
items.desc: Zero if l(a) is 0, one if l(a) is greater than 0.

items.label: M'
items.desc: Set to (M-2)/2; must not be zero.

items.label: L'
items.desc: Set to L-1; encodes the size of the length field.

viz.caption: HOW THE LENGTH OF ADDITIONAL DATA IS ENCODED

items.label: 6 octets
items.desc: For (2^16 - 2^8) <= l(a) < 2^32; followed by 4 octets of l(a).

items.label: 10 octets
items.desc: For 2^32 <= l(a) < 2^64; followed by 8 octets of l(a).
